38 Which statement about α-particles is correct?
A
α-particles emitted from a single radioactive isotope have a continuous distribution of
energies.
B
α-particles have less ionising power than β-particles.
C
The charge of an α-particle is +1.60 × 10–19
C.
D
The speeds of α-particles can be as high as 1.5 × 107
m s–1.

hints: Notice the four different properties being tested: energy spectrum from a single isotope, relative ionising power, charge in $\text{C}$, and speed in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Recall what an $\alpha$-particle is: a $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ nucleus with mass about $6.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ and charge $+2e$, and contrast discrete $\alpha$ energies with the continuous $\beta$ spectrum.
Check the numbers: $+1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ is $1e$, while $\alpha$ kinetic energies of several $\text{MeV}$ with $E = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ lead to $v$ of order $10^{7} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Identify the particle: an $\alpha$-particle is a helium-4 nucleus, $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$, with two protons and two neutrons, mass $m \approx 6.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ and charge $+2e$.

Consider the energy spectrum: $\alpha$-decay between fixed nuclear energy levels releases a fixed energy, so one isotope emits monoenergetic groups, not a continuous distribution. A continuous distribution occurs for $\beta$-decay.
Consider ionising power: because the $\alpha$-particle has large mass and charge $+2e$ and moves relatively slowly, it interacts strongly and ionises much more densely than a $\beta$-particle.

Consider charge: with two protons the charge is $q = 2 \times (+1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}) = +3.20 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so $+1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ is too small by a factor of two.

Consider speed: a typical $\alpha$ energy is $E \approx 5 \text{ MeV} \approx 8.0 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$. From $E = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, $v = \sqrt{2E/m} \approx \sqrt{2 \times 8.0 \times 10^{-13}/6.6 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{7} \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so $1.5 \times 10^{7} \text{ m s}^{-1}$ is a correct order of magnitude. This is option D.

A.explanation: Alpha decay from one isotope to a specific daughter level gives discrete energies, not a continuous spectrum. The continuous energy distribution is characteristic of $\beta$-particles where energy is shared with an antineutrino.

B.explanation: Alpha-particles have greater ionising power than $\beta$-particles because they are heavier, slower and have charge $+2e$. They produce much denser ionisation over a short range.

C.explanation: An $\alpha$-particle is a helium nucleus with two protons, so its charge is $+2e = +3.20 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$. The value $+1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ is the charge of one proton.

D.explanation: Typical $\alpha$-energies of a few $\text{MeV}$ give speeds of order $10^{7} \text{ m s}^{-1}$. A speed of $1.5 \times 10^{7} \text{ m s}^{-1}$ is about $0.05c$ and is physically reasonable.
